paper_title: EgoCaptioner: Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.

Introduction Egocentric video records how people act in and interact with their surroundings, making it valuable source of data for embodied AI and video generation [10, 15, 37, 40, 48]. Captions make these recordings searchable and allow downstream systems to identify when particular actions occur. For example, personal assistants retrieve captions as memory to answer questions about the wearers day [48], and robot learning uses timestamped action captions to curate pretraining data [15]. Both applications depend on captions that preserve the details of an activity and associate them with the right moments. Current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) [3, 22, 28, 35, 36, 4345, 52, 54? ] can produce detailed video descriptions [4, 6, 18, 52, 56]. On egocentric footage, however, they often overlook brief actions, confuse their order, misinterpret the wearers movements, or omit objects central to an event [20, 26, 32, 34, 39]. Part of the problem is that current captioners struggle to decide what to describe and how much detail each activity needs. General captioners [4, 52] cover the visible scene broadly without binding the narrative to the wearers actions. Current egocentric captioners, meanwhile, typically produce brief narration or specialize in handobject manipulation [21, 23, 47, 57], leaving activities such as navigation and social interaction less fully described. second challenge is that detail and timing are rarely achieved together. Dense paragraphs often leave unclear when individual actions begin and end, while timestamped captions typically summarize each event in sentence [12, 31] or group details by scene [50]. Furthermore, the wearers motion is difficult to interpret from the first-person viewpoint, because the body is often only partially visible, and the captioner must infer travel direction from changes in the scene [39], cues that can be misleading when head motion diverges from body motion [19]. To address these challenges, we present EgoCaptioner, which describes an egocentric video on two levels (Figure 1). video-level overview establishes the setting and spatial layout, introduces the people and objects involved, and summarizes the wearers activities and any purpose supported by the footage. Detailed steps then narrate how the activity unfolds: EgoCaptioner segments the video into temporally bounded events, divides each event into ordered steps with start and end times, and marks key moments, such as object state changes, with timestamps. This two-level structure supports three tasks: full-video captioning, overview captioning, and event-conditioned captioning, in which the model localizes and describes an event named in the instruction. We train EgoCaptioner by supervised fine-tuning on 50,000 curated examples from eight egocentric video sources, followed by reinforcement learning with rewards for factual content, temporal alignment, and caption style. We evaluate EgoCaptioner across several benchmarks on four dimensions: caption quality, captionconditioned QA, coverage of physical event details, and temporal alignment. Compared with its Qwen3.5-9B backbone, EgoCaptioner improves by 27.6 points in PhysCapBench [42] Overall, surpassing Gemini 3.1 Pro, and by 16.8 percentage points in EgoTempo [26] accuracy. It also achieves the highest PSJ score among open-source models for step segmentation on EgoHome [25]. Our ablations examine how training data scale, annotation format, and reward design each affect performance. Further analysis shows that tailoring descriptive detail to the activity helps captions capture the aspects that human observers find salient. Our contributions are as follows: 2 EgoCaptioner : Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning We formulate egocentric captioning as video overview and timed steps that captures taskfocused details, action intervals, and key moments. We develop coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline and use it to construct 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. We train EgoCaptioner with rewards for factual content, timing, and style, achieving the best open-source results on five benchmarks. 2. Related Work Multimodal Large Language Models Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) advance temporal understanding through scaled synthetic supervision [55], multi-granularity descriptions [43], and time-aware position encoding [1, 2]. Yet egocentric benchmarks reveal persistent hallucinations about object interactions [32] and temporal reasoning errors [26], calling for descriptions that faithfully ground wearer actions and camera motion in the videos temporal structure. Egocentric Video Understanding First-person video interleaves rapid head motion with hand object manipulation, making the wearer largely invisible and scene dynamics viewpoint-dependent. Representation methods address this by grouping spatiotemporal tokens into scene entities [41] or learning handobject dynamics with motion adapters [23], while captioning approaches leverage third-person references [47], cross-view transfer [21], and recursive composition across temporal scales [14]. Such captions further serve as retrievable memory for question answering [48] and as timestamped supervision for robot pretraining [15]. We produce video-level overview with timestamped steps and key moments, emphasizing hand roles, motion, and task-focused details. 3. Method 3.1. Task Formulation We describe an egocentric video at two levels. video-level overview establishes the setting and summarizes what the camera wearer is doing. Steps then narrate how the activity unfolds, organized by timed events that cover the video in consecutive, non-overlapping intervals. Overview. The overview sets the scene by describing the location, surroundings, lighting and the time of day and weather. Within this setting, it describes the wearer, other participants, and relevant objects, noting their positions relative to one another. Drawing on this context and the actions shown, it also summarizes what the wearer is doing overall and, when the goal is apparent, what they are trying to accomplish. Steps. We segment each video into non-overlapping events, each covering coherent activity, and divide each event into ordered steps with start and end times. The steps narrate what happens within the event, emphasizing the details that matter for the activity. step may also record key moment in sentence beginning with At [t], marking the instant at which something relevant happens. Tasks. The two levels define three instruction-following tasks. (1) Full-video captioning produces the overview followed by the steps of all events. (2) Overview captioning produces the overview alone. (3) Event-conditioned captioning produces the steps of an event named in the instruction, requiring the model to localize the event before describing it. 3 EgoCaptioner : Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning 3.2. Data Construction We collect egocentric videos spanning daily activities, procedural tasks, outdoor walking, and manipulation from Ego4D Goal-Step [38], the Ego4D subset of EgoHOD [23], Sekai [16], EgoVid-5M [46], the EgoPro subset of EgoSuite-Open100K [17], HumanPlus-1000 [13], the processed release of RekaDaily10k [30] and EgoLife [48]. We build the annotation coarse-to-fine with two complementary MLLMs, Gemini-3.1-Pro [9] and Seed2.1 pro [3]. Task-focused narration. Different activities call for different details, so we define four event types and use each types narration emphasis to prompt the annotator, steering the description toward the details most relevant to that activity. Handobject manipulation (manip) centers on what the wearer does to an object, each hands role, how the object changes, and where it is placed afterward. Locomotion (locomote) records the travel mode, direction, and route relative to landmarks, using camera motion cues such as bobbing or sway to identify the mode. Social interaction (social) covers who participates, how they take turns acting and responding, and what gestures or expressions clarify intent. Visual attention (attend) tracks what the wearer observes, how attention shifts between targets, and when target becomes occluded or reappears. Within step, key moments mark sudden transitions, such as an object state change, mishap, or person entering or leaving the scene. Each is written as At [t], followed by what happens at that instant. Coarse-to-fine annotation. The annotation proceeds in two stages (Figure 2(a)). (i) Structure. Gemini writes the overview from the full video. Seed2.1 pro identifies the events, their temporal boundaries and types, and an outline of steps for each event. (ii) Detail. Gemini expands each outline into timestamped step descriptions with key moments, prompted with the narration emphasis of the events type. It views an event crop with up to 1 of surrounding context on each side. Videos longer than 30 are annotated in clips of at most 30 with 0.5 overlap, and Gemini merges the clip annotations into single timeline. The two stages produce complete draft caption for verification. Verification and correction. Seed2.1 pro then reviews the draft against the full video (Figure 2(b)), jointly checking the described actions, their timing, and the consistency of the events with one another. It corrects localized errors in place, and final format check yields the validated caption. From each validated annotation we construct instructions for the three tasks in Sec. 3.1 (Figure 2(c)). For event-conditioned examples we only provide the events name without its time localization. Pose-derived motion facts. For videos with pose or trajectory recordings, we convert sensor measurements into discrete motion facts following MotionScript [51], each describing the wearers body movement or change in head-mounted viewing direction together with its temporal span. Because these facts come from sensors, they provide motion evidence independent of the reference captions and serve as additional reference facts during reinforcement learning (Sec. 3.4). 3.3. Supervised Fine-Tuning We initialize our captioning policy by supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on 50,000 curated video instructioncaption triplets, with videos up to 120 long. The training data comprise an equal mixture of full-video, overview, and event-conditioned captioning examples. This stage trains the model 4 EgoCaptioner : Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning Figure 2 Data construction pipeline. (a) Gemini-3.1-Pro and Seed2.1 pro annotate each video coarse to fine, from global overview and event outlines to timestamped steps. (b) The draft caption is reviewed against the full video and corrected. (c) Each validated caption can yield full-video, event-conditioned, and overview instructions. (d) Body and camera poses are converted into timed motion facts. to produce egocentric descriptions at the requested granularity and provides the initial policy for subsequent reinforcement learning. 3.4. Fact-based reward. We evaluate captions using four fact types defined by the caption structure in Sec. 3.1. The remaining reward details and optimization settings are provided in the supplementary material. 4. Experiments To comprehensively evaluate the ability of EgoCaptioner to produce detailed, time-aware and taskfocused descriptions, we investigate three research questions (RQs): RQ1: How well does it understand egocentric videos? RQ2: Which design choices in our annotation and training pipeline contribute to the performance? RQ3: Beyond benchmark scores, how well do its descriptions reflect the detailed, task-focused design in practice? 4.1. Experimental Setup Data and training. We initialize EgoCaptioner from Qwen3.5-9B [29] and fine-tune it with LoRA [11] (rank 32) on the data described in Sec. 3.3 for 2 epochs with learning rate of 1104. We then apply GRPO on 8,000 videoinstruction pairs balanced across the three captioning tasks, sampling 𝐺=8 rollouts per input with batch size of 32 and learning rate of 1105. Both stages use 16 GPUs. Baselines. Table 1 compares EgoCaptioner with three groups: (i) proprietary MLLMs (Gemini 3.1 Pro [9], Gemini 3.8 Flash [8], GPT-6-Astra [22]), (ii) open-source MLLMs and captioners (Qwen3-VL-8B [1], Qwen3.5-9B [29] and Qwen3.8-27B [28], Molmo2-8B [7], TimeLens-8B [53], Tarsier2-7B [52], CapRL-Video-4B [49], AVoCaDO [5]), and (iii) egocentric MLLMs (EgoThinker [24], EgoGPT [48]). Benchmarks and metrics. Inference. We uniformly sample frames across the entire video at target rate of 4 fps, capped at 240 frames. For longer videos, the effective sampling rate is reduced to preserve full temporal coverage. Within each protocol, we keep benchmark instructions and scoring fixed across models. Further details are provided in the supplementary material. 4.2. RQ1: Egocentric Video Understanding We first assess how well EgoCaptioner understands egocentric videos  (Table 1)  . The benchmarks probe two sides of this capability: how faithful and informative the descriptions are, measured by caption quality against references and by detail-oriented QA, and whether the described events are anchored to the correct moments. Description quality and video QA. EgoCaptioner delivers the strongest open-source results on EgoMe, EgoTempo, and Minerva-Ego. On EgoMe-Overview it reaches the highest BLEU-4 and METEOR among all models including proprietary ones, and on EgoMe-Steps it likewise leads in METEOR and SODA-d. EgoTempo and Minerva-Ego probe fine-grained facts such as manipulated objects, individual actions, and their order, so text-only reader can answer only when the caption records those facts. Reading from EgoCaptioners captions yields the best open-source accuracy on both benchmarks, and on Minerva-Ego it surpasses all proprietary models. On PhysCapBench, EgoCaptioner scores 78.84 Overall, the best among open-source models and above Gemini 3.1 Pro. Temporal alignment. On EgoHome, we compare our predicted steps with human-annotated subtask timelines for household activities. The permissible subsegment Jaccard (PSJ) score measures the fraction of time for which the two timelines agree on the action being performed. The judge can match step in either timeline to several finer steps in the other if their descriptions refer to the same underlying action. EgoCaptioner scores 75.51 on PSJ, ranking first among the open-source models EgoCaptioner : Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning evaluated and outperforming Gemini 3.8 Flash. Tarsier2, AVoCaDO, and EgoGPT score zero on all step-level metrics because they rarely produce parseable timestamps. Taken together, EgoCaptioner is competitive with proprietary models across all five benchmarks while being the strongest open-source model on every one of them. 4.3. RQ2: Which Design Choices Are Effective? To understand the gains in RQ1, we examine the contributions of the annotation procedure, reward design, and amount of training data. Training stages, data scale, and rewards. Table 2 reports three groups of comparisons. The first group compares the base model, SFT, and SFT followed by GRPO to show the contribution of each training stage. The second varies the amount of SFT data (10k, 25k, 50k triplets, sampled by video with the task mixture preserved) under the same recipe. The third removes one GRPO reward term at time from the full objective, keeping SFT initialization and data fixed. On our sampled subsets, SFT alone already brings large PSJ gains over the base model: even 10k triplets recover most of the PSJ improvement (67.79 vs. 71.63 at 50k), while METEOR and SODA-d improve steadily as the data scale increases to 50k. GRPO then lifts METEOR, SODA-d, and PSJ further. Without 𝑅fact, all metrics fall below the SFT initialization, as the remaining rewards supervise timing and style but place no constraint on content. Without 𝑅time, PSJ falls below SFT while METEOR is unaffected, confirming that content quality alone does not produce aligned timestamps. Without 𝑅style, SODA-d and PSJ both decrease relative to the full objective. Notably, PSJ responds to all three ablations: it credits step only when its description matches the video and its interval aligns with the reference, PSJ reflects both content and temporal fidelity. Coarse-to-fine annotation. To isolate the effect of our multi-stage annotation pipeline on data quality, we construct single-pass baseline: we prompt Gemini 3.1 Pro to generate complete caption in our target format from single call per video, bypassing the intermediate event segmentation and per-event description stages. The two conditions share the same source videos, training volume, output format, and training hyperparameters; the single-pass prompt is detailed in the supplementary material. As shown in Table 3, the coarse-to-fine supervision improves every metric. The largest gains appear on detail-oriented QA, where EgoTempo accuracy rises by nearly 10 points and Minerva-Ego more than doubles, and on temporal alignment, where PSJ rises by about 9 points. In the singlepass condition the annotator segments and describes each step in one reading, producing coarser boundaries and fewer step-level facts. Our procedure fixes the event structure first and then describes each step from its event crop, which yields both aligned boundaries and the fine-grained facts. 4.4. RQ3: Detailed and Task-Focused in Practice? We examine two questions about what the captions contain in practice: whether the activity-type narration emphasis produces different details for different activities, and whether the quality gains come from denser information per token rather than simply longer output. Task-focused detail. Figure 4 illustrates how EgoCaptioner shifts its descriptive focus to match the wearers activity. For manipulation, the caption decomposes continuous action into atomic steps, preserving the purpose and target of each motion. We compare EgoCaptioner with CapRL-Video-4B, the strongest captioner baseline on the egocentric subset of PhysCapBench, across all seven evaluation dimensions (Figure 5). The two models produce captions of comparable mean length (both 548 words 10 EgoCaptioner : Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning Figure 5 Per-dimension PhysCapBench scores (RQ3). EgoCaptioner vs. CapRL-Video-4B at comparable caption length. EC: event coverage, OR: objects and roles, AM: actions and motion, CI: contact and interaction, SO: states and outcomes, MC: physical mechanisms and causality, TO: temporal order. per video), so differences reflect the information each word carries rather than sheer verbosity. At this length, EgoCaptioner leads on every dimension, with the largest gains in physical mechanisms and causality (+5.88 points) and temporal order (+4.57 points). For reader reconstructing procedure from text, knowing which actions came first and how they caused the observed changes is exactly what separates usable caption from list of observations. This suggests that EgoCaptioners captions can serve as practical text interface to egocentric video, enabling applications such as step-by-step instruction generation and activity summarization. 5. Conclusion We presented EgoCaptioner, an egocentric video captioner trained with coarse-to-fine supervision and reinforcement learning that jointly optimizes factual content, temporal alignment, and caption style. EgoCaptioner achieves the strongest open-source results on five egocentric benchmarks and is competitive with proprietary models across caption quality, detail-oriented QA, and temporal alignment. Ablations show that coarse-to-fine annotation, which establishes event structure before step descriptions, and joint optimization of factual and temporal rewards are both necessary for consistent gains. Per-dimension analysis on PhysCapBench further reveals that task-focused narration contributes most where understanding causality and temporal order is required, not merely naming visible objects.
